title: By what authority? (Mark 11:27–33)
hook: leaders try to trap him, and he answers with a question

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith that moves mountains, and a surprising condition. Your line was forgive, then pray. Did you check your hand for a grudge? Day two hundred nine.

"Have you stopped being late all the time?" Some questions aren't really questions. Whatever you say, you lose. Jesus is back in Jerusalem, walking in the temple courts, the day after he overturned the tables. And a delegation arrives: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders. In the King James Bible they ask: "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things?" It's a trap with two jaws. If he says God gave it to me, they could call it blasphemy. If he says no one, then he's just a troublemaker from Galilee. And the crowd is listening.
screen: `A QUESTION THAT'S A TRAP.` → `THE COUNCIL ARRIVES.` → `WHO GAVE THEE THIS AUTHORITY?`

segments.voice: Jesus says: let me ask you one question. Answer me, and I'll tell you by what authority I do these things. Then: "The baptism of John, was it from heaven, or of men? answer me." Now they're the ones in the trap. They huddle. If we say from heaven, he'll say, then why didn't you believe him? If we say from men, the crowd will turn on us, because, as Mark puts it, all men counted John a prophet indeed. So they give the safest answer there is: "We cannot tell." We don't know. And Jesus says: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things." Notice this isn't a dodge. His question and theirs are the same question. John had baptized him, and the voice from heaven had spoken at that very moment. If they could be honest about John, they'd have their answer about Jesus. Jesus answers with a question again and again in the Gospels. Who do you say I am? What do you want? Why are you afraid? A good question doesn't close the conversation. It hands it back and asks you to be honest. Mark lets us overhear what the leaders weigh: the crowd, not John. The word for authority in Greek is exousia: the right, and the power, to act.
screen: `LET ME ASK YOU ONE QUESTION.` · `JOHN: FROM HEAVEN, OR OF MEN?` · `WE CANNOT TELL.` · `A QUESTION HANDS IT BACK.` · then, large: `NEITHER DO I TELL YOU BY WHAT AUTHORITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a good question. Settle, and breathe. Think of a hard question someone's been pressing on you. At work, at home, in your own head. Instead of rushing to answer it, ask what question lies underneath. What are you really asking? What would help? What do you think? What are you afraid of? Find one honest question you could hand back, not to escape, but to open things up. If you pray, you can bring God your own hardest question. The bell holds the time.
By what authority? The leaders' trap, answered with a question about John that they were afraid to answer honestly.
Your line: answer with a question. Today, when someone asks you something hard, ask one good question back before you answer. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christians often notice how many questions Jesus asks in the Gospels, and some Bible study groups use his questions, like "who do you say I am?", as prompts for honest discussion.

myth: Jesus refused to answer because he had no answer
his question about John was the answer, if they'd been honest.
everyone held John to have been a real prophet.
the leaders talked it over before they answered
Mark lets us hear them reason: if we say from heaven... if we say of men...

fork.setup: you're a leader who has asked Jesus: by what authority? he asks back: was John's baptism from heaven, or of men? the crowd is listening. what do you say?
fork.reveal: they choose "We cannot tell." and he replies: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things."

original.note: Greek: authority, the right and power to act. the word in the leaders' question in Mark 11:28.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus dodged a hard question.
what it means: he hands back a question that would answer theirs, if they'd be honest about John.
what a scholar hears: exousia, the right to act; and John's baptism is where Mark's gospel first has the voice from heaven speak (1:11).

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Cut the unsourced "three groups who together led the city's highest council", "hundreds of questions" and the general claim about Jewish teaching style; removed the preacher's etymology of exousia ("what comes out of who you are") from teach, original note and trapdoor; fixed the garbled trapdoor line ("where Mark first heard the voice"); "everyone holds John" now follows Mark 11:32; the leaders' motive is shown from the text rather than judged ("they were asking to win"); hook no longer tells the listener what they've experienced; one myth item replaced.
Chief priests, scribes and elders as the three groups of the Sanhedrin; confirm phrasing 'the city's highest council'.
'Hundreds of questions': popular counts (e.g. about 300 questions asked by Jesus in the Gospels) vary. Kept vague on purpose.
The etymology of exousia (ex + ousia/einai) is given loosely as 'what comes out of who you are'; confirm or soften.
Answering a question with a question as a Jewish teaching style: stated generally; confirm.
